notes.headline: Sumitomo Mitsui: half-year profit up 7.5% to ¥1.0 trillion; full-year forecast set at a record ¥1.9 trillion after a 2-for-1 split
notes.takeaway: Profit for the six months to September rose 7.5% to ¥1.0 trillion, slower than its two big rivals because of losses on its bond portfolio. SMFG still raised its full-year forecast to ¥1.9 trillion, up 20%, lifted its dividend, and the ADRs gained 1.5%.
results: Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group reported profit attributable to shareholders of ¥1,003.2 billion for the six months ended September 30, up 7.5%, on ordinary income of ¥5,800.1 billion, up 11.4%. Ordinary profit rose 9.2% to ¥1,395.6 billion. On a per-ADS basis the quarter came to about US$0.25, in line with the consensus.

Comprehensive income fell 41.6% to ¥601.8 billion, reflecting lower valuations on the group’s bond and equity holdings as Japanese yields rose. At the holding-company level, ordinary profit rose 35% on higher dividends from subsidiaries.

On October 1 SMFG split its shares two for one. The full-year dividend forecast is ¥200 on the old basis, equivalent to ¥100 after the split, and the earnings forecast assumes continued share repurchases.
mgmt: SMFG revised its May forecast and now expects profit attributable to shareholders of ¥1.9 trillion for the year to March 2027, an increase of 20% and a record, equal to ¥250.84 a share after the split. The half-year result is 53% of that figure, implying a stronger second half.
The company also revised its dividend forecast upward and noted that the earnings-per-share forecast reflects both the stock split and buybacks. It deconsolidated JRI Holdings during the period.
view: SMFG’s first half was the weakest of the three megabanks, and the reason is the bond book rather than the franchise. Rising yen rates lift lending margins but reduce the value of bonds bought when yields were zero, and SMFG has been taking those losses through its income statement and comprehensive income more aggressively than peers. That depresses reported growth today and raises future interest income; it is a timing choice, not a sign of weakness.

The forecast is the more telling number. A 20% increase to ¥1.9 trillion with only 53% delivered in the first half means management expects the second half to be markedly better as repriced loans and reinvested bonds start earning more. SMFG has a record of setting forecasts it then beats, and the stock split and buyback language suggest a board that wants to broaden its shareholder base and keep returning capital.

Compared with MUFG and Mizuho, SMFG is the purer play on domestic corporate lending and on its growing Asian franchise in India, Indonesia and Vietnam, where it has bought stakes in local lenders. Those stakes add growth but also emerging-market credit risk. The valuation gap with MUFG has narrowed; what would widen it again is a stumble in Asia or a pause by the Bank of Japan.
notes.watch: Watch the second-half run rate against the ¥1.9 trillion forecast, further bond-portfolio losses, and the size of the next buyback at the full-year results.
